\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}


In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.

The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
the origin).
This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
the theorem,
no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
That changed with the publication of
\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
Gaussians.
Walther's proof depends on
a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
of Walther's proof.
By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
calculations.

A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
to every point, $x$.
We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
yields a constant times $\mu$.
Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.

\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}


Let $\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \subset\R^n$.

\proclaim The Cram\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
probability measures on $\R^n$ such that $\mu(S) = \nu(S)$ for all $S \in
\hfsp$. Then $\mu = \nu$.

\proof
Let
$\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\hfsp$ 
that is invariant under isometries, normalized so that
$$
\sigma\big(\{0 \in S, x \notin S\}\big) = \|x\|/2
\label e.distance
$$
for $\|x\|= 1$.
The measure $\sigma$ goes back to \ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it
can be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \ref b.SW:book/ for
a generalization.)
Let $\sfc_{n-1}$ denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
$\sphere^{n-1} \subset \R^n$, and let
$\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\R$.
Write $\varphi \colon \sphere^{n-1} \times \R \to \hfsp$ for the map
$$
\varphi(\omega, p)
:=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
\,.
$$
Then $\sigma := \alpha_n \cdot \varphi_*(\sfc_{n-1} \times \lambda)$ for some
constant $\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.
It is clear that $\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin
and under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.
Translation invariance
amounts to the property that for $y \in \R^n$, the pushforward by
$\varphi_y(\omega, p) := \varphi(\omega, p) - y$ is the same measure. But
since 
$$\eqaln{
\varphi(\omega, p) - y 
&= 
\bigl\{ x - y \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, {x + y} \ge p \bigr\}
\cr&=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p - \ip \omega, y \bigr\}
=
\varphi\bigl(\omega, p - \ip \omega, y\bigr)
\,,
}$$
isometry invariance of $\lambda$ gives this property.
The isometry invariance of $\sigma$ implies that $\sigma\big(\{0 \in S,\, x
\notin S\}\big)$ is a function of $\|x\|$ alone; additivity for collinear
segments shows that it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose $\alpha_n$
so that \ref e.distance/ holds.

From \ref e.distance/ and isometry invariance, we have
$$
\|x\| =
\int_\hfsp |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
Integrating with respect to a
signed measure $\mu$ on $\R^n$ with compact support, we obtain
$$
\int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \int_{\R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\mu(x) \,d\sigma(S)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[1_S(0)\big(1 - 2\mu(S)\big) + \mu(S)\Bigr] \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another
choice and subtracting, we get
$$
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\bigr)\bigl(1 - 2\mu(S)\bigr)\Bigr]
\,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed
measure, $\mu$.

Define
$$
f_\mu(y)
:=
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
\,.
$$
We have shown that the function $S \mapsto \mu(S)$ determines $f_\mu$. It
remains to show that $f_\mu$ determines $\mu$.

The idea is that if $n = 2m-1$ is odd, then $\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m
\mu$ for some constant $c_m$, using the fundamental solution of the
Laplacian, $\Delta$. This then establishes the Cram\'er--Wold theorem
in odd dimensions.
But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension, 
the Cram\'er--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well.
That is, we may identify a measure $\mu$ on $\R^{2m}$ with a measure $\mu'$
on $\R^{2m} \times \{0\} \subset \R^{2m+1}$. 
%Note that values on closed
%half-spaces determine values on open half-spaces by continuity.
%Thus, 
The function $S \mapsto
\mu(S)$ on half-spaces $S \subset \R^{2m}$ determines the values
$\mu'(S')$ for half-spaces $S' \subset \R^{2m+1}$. Since this determines
$\mu'$, the theorem follows for $\mu$.

\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y) 
&=
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} (\Delta^m g)(y) \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,
d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
\cr&=
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} g(y) \Delta_y^m \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,
d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
\cr&=
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} c_m g(x) \,d\mu(x)
\,.
}$$
\fi

We now show that
$\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m \mu$ in an appropriate sense for $\mu$ on $\R^{2m-1}$.
Recall Green's second identity, which says that for a
bounded domain $D \subset \R^n$ with $C^1$ boundary $\partial D$ having
outward unit normal $\n$ and two functions $\phi, \psi \in C^2(\overlinesl
D\,)$, we
have
$$
\int_D (\phi \Delta \psi - \psi \Delta \phi) 
=
\int_{\partial D} (\phi \nabla_\n \psi - \psi \nabla_\n \phi)
\,.
$$
Recall also that if $F \colon \R^n \to \R$ is such that $F(x) =
G\bigl(\|x\|\bigr)$ depends only on $r := \|x\|$, then 
$$
(\Delta F)(x)
=
G''(r) + {n-1 \over r} G'(r)
\,.
$$
In particular, $\Delta r^k = k (k + n - 2) r^{k-2}$.
If the support of $\psi$ lies in the interior of a ball $B(\bfz, R)$ 
and $\phi(x) = r^k$ with $k > -n + 2$, then letting $D$ be $B(\bfz,
R) \setminus B(\bfz, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon \to 0$ shows that
$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \int_{\R^n} \psi \Delta \phi$. Similarly,
if $k = - n +2$, then 
$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \beta_{n-1} \psi(\bfz)$, where
$\beta_{n-1}$ is the surface area of $\sphere^{n-1}$.

To show that $f_\mu$
determines $\int g \,d\mu$ for all $g \in C^\infty_{\csp}(\R^{2m-1})$, we
now prove that with $c_m := 2(-2\pi)^{m-1} (2m-2)!!$, where $!!$ denotes
the double factorial, we have
$$
\int g \,d\mu = c_m^{-1}
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y)
\,,
$$
where now
$\lambda$ denotes Lebesgue measure on $\R^{2m-1}$. Fubini's theorem
yields
$$
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y) 
=
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
\, d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
\,.
$$
Applying the preceding Green formulas (translated to $x$)
repeatedly to the inner integral, we obtain
$$\eqaln{
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
\, d\lambda(y) 
&=
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \Delta_y^{m-1}
\big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \Delta g(y) \,
d\lambda(y) 
\cr&=
c_m g(x) 
\,,
}$$
as desired.
\Qed

\eject

Our inversion formula $\mu = c_m^{-1} \Delta^m f_\mu$ in $\R^{2m-1}$
is similar to a well-known inversion formula for the Radon
transform due to \ref b.Radon/ and \ref b.John:book/, p.~13:
If $f \in C^1_{\csp}(\R^n)$, then writing $J(\omega, p) := \int_{\langle
\omega, x \rangle = p} f(x) \,dx$ for the integral of $f$ on a hyperplane
perpendicular to $\omega\in \sphere^{n-1}$, we have
$$
f(x) = \cases{\vadjust{\kern1pt}%
{1 \over 2} (2\pi)^{1-n} (-\Delta_x)^{(n-1)/2}
\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} J(\omega,\langle\omega, x\rangle)\,
d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
odd\cr
- (2\pi)^{-n} (-\Delta_x)^{(n-2)/2}
\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} \int_\R {dJ(\omega, p) \over p - \langle\omega,
x\rangle}\, d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
even.\cr}
$$
%(Here, we are integrating with respect to unnormalized area measure.)
%This is from Helgason's remarks; in his book, he has a factor of 1/2 for
%the even case as well. John does not have the 1/2, but he has a large typo
%for $n$ odd.
Apparently it was not realized until pointed out by \ref b.Renyi/ that the
theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ generalized the injectivity
results of Radon, John, and others.

The injectivity of the map $\mu \mapsto \int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)$ for
probability measures $\mu$ with finite first moment holds in other spaces
as well. On metric spaces of negative type, it is equivalent to strong
negative type. See Remark 3.4 of \ref b.L:dcov/ for details and references.
That paper also shows its relevance to statistics.

\title{A Calculus Proof of the Cram\'er--Wold Theorem}

\author{Russell Lyons and Kevin Zumbrun}

\abstract{We present a short, elementary proof not involving Fourier transforms
of the theorem of Cram\'er and Wold that a Borel probability measure is
determined by its values on half-spaces.
}


\bottomII{Primary 
60E10. %Characteristic functions; other transforms
Secondary
44A12, %Radon transform
53C65. %Integral geometry
}
{Distributions of probability measures, Radon transform, integral geometry.}
{Research partially supported by NSF grants DMS-1007244 and DMS-1400555.}

\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}


In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.

The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
the origin).
This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
the theorem,
no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
That changed with the publication of
\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
Gaussians.
Walther's proof depends on
a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
of Walther's proof.
By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
calculations.

A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
to every point, $x$.
We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
yields a constant times $\mu$.
Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.

\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}


Let $\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \subset\R^n$.

\proclaim The Cram\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
probability measures on $\R^n$ such that $\mu(S) = \nu(S)$ for all $S \in
\hfsp$. Then $\mu = \nu$.

\proof
Let
$\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\hfsp$ 
that is invariant under isometries, normalized so that
$$
\sigma\big(\{0 \in S, x \notin S\}\big) = \|x\|/2
\label e.distance
$$
for $\|x\|= 1$.
The measure $\sigma$ goes back to \ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it
can be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \ref b.SW:book/ for
a generalization.)
Let $\sfc_{n-1}$ denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
$\sphere^{n-1} \subset \R^n$, and let
$\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\R$.
Write $\varphi \colon \sphere^{n-1} \times \R \to \hfsp$ for the map
$$
\varphi(\omega, p)
:=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
\,.
$$
Then $\sigma := \alpha_n \cdot \varphi_*(\sfc_{n-1} \times \lambda)$ for some
constant $\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.
It is clear that $\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin
and under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.
Translation invariance
amounts to the property that for $y \in \R^n$, the pushforward by
$\varphi_y(\omega, p) := \varphi(\omega, p) - y$ is the same measure. But
since 
$$\eqaln{
\varphi(\omega, p) - y 
&= 
\bigl\{ x - y \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, {x + y} \ge p \bigr\}
\cr&=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p - \ip \omega, y \bigr\}
=
\varphi\bigl(\omega, p - \ip \omega, y\bigr)
\,,
}$$
isometry invariance of $\lambda$ gives this property.
The isometry invariance of $\sigma$ implies that $\sigma\big(\{0 \in S,\, x
\notin S\}\big)$ is a function of $\|x\|$ alone; additivity for collinear
segments shows that it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose $\alpha_n$
so that \ref e.distance/ holds.

From \ref e.distance/ and isometry invariance, we have
$$
\|x\| =
\int_\hfsp |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
Integrating with respect to a
signed measure $\mu$ on $\R^n$ with compact support, we obtain
$$
\int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \int_{\R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\mu(x) \,d\sigma(S)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[1_S(0)\big(1 - 2\mu(S)\big) + \mu(S)\Bigr] \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another
choice and subtracting, we get
$$
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\bigr)\bigl(1 - 2\mu(S)\bigr)\Bigr]
\,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed
measure, $\mu$.

Define
$$
f_\mu(y)
:=
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
\,.
$$
We have shown that the function $S \mapsto \mu(S)$ determines $f_\mu$. It
remains to show that $f_\mu$ determines $\mu$.

The idea is that if $n = 2m-1$ is odd, then $\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m
\mu$ for some constant $c_m$, using the fundamental solution of the
Laplacian, $\Delta$. This then establishes the Cram\'er--Wold theorem
in odd dimensions.
But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension, 
the Cram\'er--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well.
That is, we may identify a measure $\mu$ on $\R^{2m}$ with a measure $\mu'$
on $\R^{2m} \times \{0\} \subset \R^{2m+1}$. 
%Note that values on closed
%half-spaces determine values on open half-spaces by continuity.
%Thus, 
The function $S \mapsto
\mu(S)$ on half-spaces $S \subset \R^{2m}$ determines the values
$\mu'(S')$ for half-spaces $S' \subset \R^{2m+1}$. Since this determines
$\mu'$, the theorem follows for $\mu$.

   193|\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}
   194|
   195|
   196|In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
   197|transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.
   198|
   199|The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
   200|measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
   201|assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
   202|the origin).
   203|This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
   204|generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
   205|textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
   206|the theorem,
   207|no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
   208|That changed with the publication of
   209|\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
   210|Gaussians.
   211|Walther's proof depends on
   212|a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
   213|calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
   214|of Walther's proof.
   215|By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
   216|calculations.
   217|
   218|A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
   219|Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
   220|for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
   221|to every point, $x$.
   222|We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
   223|yields a constant times $\mu$.
   224|Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.
   225|
   226|\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}
   227|
   228|
   229|Let $\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \subset\R^n$.
   230|
   231|\proclaim The Cram\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
   232|probability measures on $\R^n$ such that $\mu(S) = \nu(S)$ for all $S \in
   233|\hfsp$. Then $\mu = \nu$.
   234|
   235|\proof
   236|Let
   237|$\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\hfsp$ 
   238|that is invariant under isometries, normalized so that
   239|$$
   240|\sigma\big(\{0 \in S, x \notin S\}\big) = \|x\|/2
   241|\label e.distance
   242|$$
   243|for $\|x\|= 1$.
   244|The measure $\sigma$ goes back to \ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it
   245|can be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \ref b.SW:book/ for
   246|a generalization.)
   247|Let $\sfc_{n-1}$ denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
   248|$\sphere^{n-1} \subset \R^n$, and let
   249|$\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\R$.
   250|Write $\varphi \colon \sphere^{n-1} \times \R \to \hfsp$ for the map
   251|$$
   252|\varphi(\omega, p)
   253|:=
   254|\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
   255|\,.
   256|$$
   257|Then $\sigma := \alpha_n \cdot \varphi_*(\sfc_{n-1} \times \lambda)$ for some
   258|constant $\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.
   259|It is clear that $\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin
   260|and under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.
   261|Translation invariance
   262|amounts to the property that for $y \in \R^n$, the pushforward by
   263|$\varphi_y(\omega, p) := \varphi(\omega, p) - y$ is the same measure. But
   264|since 
   265|$$\eqaln{
   266|\varphi(\omega, p) - y 
   267|&= 
   268|\bigl\{ x - y \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
   269|=
   270|\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, {x + y} \ge p \bigr\}
   271|\cr&=
   272|\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p - \ip \omega, y \bigr\}
   273|=
   274|\varphi\bigl(\omega, p - \ip \omega, y\bigr)
   275|\,,
   276|}$$
   277|isometry invariance of $\lambda$ gives this property.
   278|The isometry invariance of $\sigma$ implies that $\sigma\big(\{0 \in S,\, x
   279|\notin S\}\big)$ is a function of $\|x\|$ alone; additivity for collinear
   280|segments shows that it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose $\alpha_n$
   281|so that \ref e.distance/ holds.
   282|
   283|From \ref e.distance/ and isometry invariance, we have
   284|$$
   285|\|x\| =
   286|\int_\hfsp |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\sigma(S)
   287|\,.
   288|$$
   289|Integrating with respect to a
   290|signed measure $\mu$ on $\R^n$ with compact support, we obtain
   291|$$
   292|\int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)
   293|=
   294|\int_\hfsp \int_{\R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\mu(x) \,d\sigma(S)
   295|=
   296|\int_\hfsp \Bigl[1_S(0)\big(1 - 2\mu(S)\big) + \mu(S)\Bigr] \,d\sigma(S)
   297|\,.
   298|$$
   299|The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another
   300|choice and subtracting, we get
   301|$$
   302|\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
   303|=
   304|\int_\hfsp \Bigl[\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\bigr)\bigl(1 - 2\mu(S)\bigr)\Bigr]
   305|\,d\sigma(S)
   306|\,.
   307|$$
   308|By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed
   309|measure, $\mu$.
   310|
   311|Define

   313|f_\mu(y)
   314|:=
   315|\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
   316|\,.
   317|$$
   318|We have shown that the function $S \mapsto \mu(S)$ determines $f_\mu$. It
   319|remains to show that $f_\mu$ determines $\mu$.
   320|
   321|The idea is that if $n = 2m-1$ is odd, then $\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m
   322|\mu$ for some constant $c_m$, using the fundamental solution of the
   323|Laplacian, $\Delta$. This then establishes the Cram\'er--Wold theorem
   324|in odd dimensions.
   325|But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension, 
   326|the Cram\'er--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well.
   327|That is, we may identify a measure $\mu$ on $\R^{2m}$ with a measure $\mu'$
   328|on $\R^{2m} \times \{0\} \subset \R^{2m+1}$.

   330|%half-spaces determine values on open half-spaces by continuity.
   331|%Thus, 
   332|The function $S \mapsto
   333|\mu(S)$ on half-spaces $S \subset \R^{2m}$ determines the values
   334|$\mu'(S')$ for half-spaces $S' \subset \R^{2m+1}$. Since this determines
   335|$\mu'$, the theorem follows for $\mu$.

   338|To prove this, it suffices to show that $f_\mu$
   339|determines $\int g \,d\mu$ for all $g \in C^\infty_{\csp}(\R^{2m-1})$. I claim
   340|that if $\Delta^m r = c_m \delta_0$, then $\int g \,d\mu = c_m^{-1}
   341|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y)$. Indeed,
   342|$$\eqaln{
   343|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y) 
   344|&=
   345|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} (\Delta^m g)(y) \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,
   346|d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
   347|\cr&=
   348|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} g(y) \Delta_y^m \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,
   349|d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
   350|\cr&=
   351|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} c_m g(x) \,d\mu(x)
   352|\,.
   353|}$$
   354|\fi
   355|
   356|We now show that
   357|$\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m \mu$ in an appropriate sense for $\mu$ on $\R^{2m-1}$.
   358|Recall Green's second identity, which says that for a
   359|bounded domain $D \subset \R^n$ with $C^1$ boundary $\partial D$ having
   360|outward unit normal $\n$ and two functions $\phi, \psi \in C^2(\overlinesl
   361|D\,)$, we
   362|have
   363|$$
   364|\int_D (\phi \Delta \psi - \psi \Delta \phi) 
   365|=
   366|\int_{\partial D} (\phi \nabla_\n \psi - \psi \nabla_\n \phi)
   367|\,.
   368|$$
   369|Recall also that if $F \colon \R^n \to \R$ is such that $F(x) =
   370|G\bigl(\|x\|\bigr)$ depends only on $r := \|x\|$, then 
   371|$$
   372|(\Delta F)(x)
   373|=
   374|G''(r) + {n-1 \over r} G'(r)
   375|\,.
   376|$$
   377|In particular, $\Delta r^k = k (k + n - 2) r^{k-2}$.
   378|If the support of $\psi$ lies in the interior of a ball $B(\bfz, R)$ 
   379|and $\phi(x) = r^k$ with $k > -n + 2$, then letting $D$ be $B(\bfz,
   380|R) \setminus B(\bfz, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon \to 0$ shows that
   381|$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \int_{\R^n} \psi \Delta \phi$. Similarly,
   382|if $k = - n +2$, then 
   383|$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \beta_{n-1} \psi(\bfz)$, where
   384|$\beta_{n-1}$ is the surface area of $\sphere^{n-1}$.
   385|
   386|To show that $f_\mu$
   387|determines $\int g \,d\mu$ for all $g \in C^\infty_{\csp}(\R^{2m-1})$, we
   388|now prove that with $c_m := 2(-2\pi)^{m-1} (2m-2)!!$, where $!!$ denotes
   389|the double factorial, we have
   390|$$
   391|\int g \,d\mu = c_m^{-1}
   392|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y)
   393|\,,
   394|$$
   395|where now
   396|$\lambda$ denotes Lebesgue measure on $\R^{2m-1}$. Fubini's theorem
   397|yields
   398|$$
   399|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y) 
   400|=
   401|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
   402|\, d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
   403|\,.
   404|$$
   405|Applying the preceding Green formulas (translated to $x$)
   406|repeatedly to the inner integral, we obtain
   407|$$\eqaln{
   408|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
   409|\, d\lambda(y) 
   410|&=
   411|\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \Delta_y^{m-1}
   412|\big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \Delta g(y) \,
   413|d\lambda(y) 
   414|\cr&=
   415|c_m g(x) 
   416|\,,
   417|}$$
   418|as desired.
   419|\Qed
   420|
   421|\eject
   422|
   423|Our inversion formula $\mu = c_m^{-1} \Delta^m f_\mu$ in $\R^{2m-1}$
   424|is similar to a well-known inversion formula for the Radon
   425|transform due to \ref b.Radon/ and \ref b.John:book/, p.~13:
   426|If $f \in C^1_{\csp}(\R^n)$, then writing $J(\omega, p) := \int_{\langle
   427|\omega, x \rangle = p} f(x) \,dx$ for the integral of $f$ on a hyperplane
   428|perpendicular to $\omega\in \sphere^{n-1}$, we have
   429|$$
   430|f(x) = \cases{\vadjust{\kern1pt}%
   431|{1 \over 2} (2\pi)^{1-n} (-\Delta_x)^{(n-1)/2}
   432|\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} J(\omega,\langle\omega, x\rangle)\,
   433|d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
   434|odd\cr
   435|- (2\pi)^{-n} (-\Delta_x)^{(n-2)/2}
   436|\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} \int_\R {dJ(\omega, p) \over p - \langle\omega,
   437|x\rangle}\, d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
   438|even.\cr}
   439|$$
   440|%(Here, we are integrating with respect to unnormalized area measure.)
   441|%This is from Helgason's remarks; in his book, he has a factor of 1/2 for
   442|%the even case as well. John does not have the 1/2, but he has a large typo
   443|%for $n$ odd.
   444|Apparently it was not realized until pointed out by \ref b.Renyi/ that the
   445|theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ generalized the injectivity
   446|results of Radon, John, and others.
   447|
   448|The injectivity of the map $\mu \mapsto \int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)$ for

   450|as well. On metric spaces of negative type, it is equivalent to strong
   451|negative type. See Remark 3.4 of \ref b.L:dcov/ for details and references.

   194|The source proof of the proclaimed theorem is available and should be used by the prover. It is reproduced here from the TeX/PDF extraction, with minor whitespace normalization only.

   196|```text
   197|Let S be the set of closed half-spaces S ⊂ R^n.
   198|
   199|The Cramer--Wold Theorem. Let μ and ν be Borel probability measures on R^n such that
   200|μ(S) = ν(S) for all S ∈ S. Then μ = ν.
   201|
   202|Proof. Let σ be the (infinite) Borel measure on S that is invariant under isometries,
   203|normalized so that
   204|
   205|  σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) = ‖x‖/2                                      (2.1)
   206|
   207|for ‖x‖ = 1. The measure σ goes back to Crofton (1868) (in two dimensions); it can be
   208|constructed as follows. Let Ω_{n-1} denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
   209|S^{n-1} ⊂ R^n, and let λ denote Lebesgue measure on R. Write
   210|ϕ : S^{n-1} × R → S for the map
   211|
   212|  ϕ(ω,p) := {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}.
   213|
   214|Then σ := α_n · ϕ_*(Ω_{n-1} × λ) for some constant α_n whose value does not concern us.
   215|It is clear that σ is invariant under rotations about the origin and under reflections in
   216|hyperplanes that pass through the origin. Translation invariance amounts to the property
   217|that for y ∈ R^n, the pushforward by ϕ_y(ω,p) := ϕ(ω,p) - y is the same measure. But since
   218|
   219|  ϕ(ω,p) - y
   220|    = {x - y ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}
   221|    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x + y> ≥ p}
   222|    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p - <ω,y>}
   223|    = ϕ(ω, p - <ω,y>),
   224|
   225|isometry invariance of λ gives this property. The isometry invariance of σ implies that
   226|σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) is a function of ‖x‖ alone; additivity for collinear segments shows that
   227|it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose α_n so that (2.1) holds.
   228|
   229|From (2.1) and isometry invariance, we have
   230|
   231|  ‖x‖ = ∫_S |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dσ(S).
   232|
   233|Integrating with respect to a signed measure μ on R^n with compact support, we obtain
   234|
   235|  ∫_{R^n} ‖x‖ dμ(x)
   236|    = ∫_S ∫_{R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dμ(x) dσ(S)
   237|    = ∫_S [1_S(0)(1 - 2 μ(S)) + μ(S)] dσ(S).
   238|
   239|The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another choice and subtracting, we get
   240|
   241|  ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x)
   242|    = ∫_S [(1_S(y) - 1_S(0))(1 - 2 μ(S))] dσ(S).
   243|
   244|By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed measure μ.
   245|
   246|Define
   247|
   248|  f_μ(y) := ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x).
   249|
   250|We have shown that the function S ↦ μ(S) determines f_μ. It remains to show that f_μ
   251|determines μ.
   252|
   253|The idea is that if n = 2m - 1 is odd, then Δ^m f_μ = c_m μ for some constant c_m, using
   254|the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, Δ. This then establishes the Cramer--Wold
   255|theorem in odd dimensions. But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension,
   256|the Cramer--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well. That is, we may identify a
   257|measure μ on R^{2m} with a measure μ' on R^{2m} × {0} ⊂ R^{2m+1}. The function S ↦ μ(S)
   258|on half-spaces S ⊂ R^{2m} determines the values μ'(S') for half-spaces S' ⊂ R^{2m+1}.
   259|Since this determines μ', the theorem follows for μ.
   260|
   261|We now show that Δ^m f_μ = c_m μ in an appropriate sense for μ on R^{2m-1}. Recall Green's
   262|second identity, which says that for a bounded domain D ⊂ R^n with C^1 boundary ∂D having
   263|outward unit normal n and two functions φ, ψ ∈ C^2(closure D), we have
   264|
   265|  ∫_D (φ Δψ - ψ Δφ) = ∫_{∂D} (φ ∇_n ψ - ψ ∇_n φ).
   266|
   267|Recall also that if F : R^n → R is such that F(x) = G(‖x‖) depends only on r := ‖x‖, then
   268|
   269|  (ΔF)(x) = G''(r) + ((n-1)/r) G'(r).
   270|
   271|In particular, Δ r^k = k(k+n-2) r^{k-2}. If the support of ψ lies in the interior of a ball
   272|B(0,R) and φ(x) = r^k with k > -n+2, then letting D be B(0,R) \ B(0,ε) with ε → 0 shows
   273|that
   274|
   275|  ∫_{R^n} φ Δψ = ∫_{R^n} ψ Δφ.
   276|
   277|Similarly, if k = -n+2, then
   278|
   279|  ∫_{R^n} φ Δψ = β_{n-1} ψ(0),
   280|
   281|where β_{n-1} is the surface area of S^{n-1}.
   282|
   283|To show that f_μ determines ∫ g dμ for all g ∈ C_c^∞(R^{2m-1}), we now prove that with
   284|c_m := 2(-2π)^{m-1}(2m-2)!!, where !! denotes the double factorial, we have
   285|
   286|  ∫ g dμ = c_m^{-1} ∫_{R^{2m-1}} f_μ(y) (Δ^m g)(y) dλ(y),
   287|
   288|where now λ denotes Lebesgue measure on R^{2m-1}. Fubini's theorem yields
   289|
   290|  ∫_{R^{2m-1}} f_μ(y) (Δ^m g)(y) dλ(y)
   291|    = ∫_{R^{2m-1}} ∫_{R^{2m-1}} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) (Δ^m g)(y) dλ(y) dμ(x).
   292|
   293|Applying the preceding Green formulas (translated to x) repeatedly to the inner integral,

                                                In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier transforms, of a

                                                     Abstract. We present a short, elementary proof not involving Fourier transforms
                                                     of the theorem of Cramér and Wold that a Borel probability measure is determined
                                                     by its values on half-spaces.




                                                                                     §1. Introduction.
                                                In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier transforms, of a
                                           theorem of Cramér and Wold.
                                                The fundamental theorem of Cramér and Wold (1936) states that a Borel probability
                                           measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently,
                                           by its projections to lines through the origin). This theorem is proved easily with the aid of
                                           Fourier analysis. However, generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
                                           textbook of Billingsley (1995) that despite the elementary statement of the theorem, no proof
                                           was known that did not use Fourier transforms. That changed with the publication of Walther
                                           (1997), who used Gaussians. Walther’s proof depends on a nice idea, but its implementation
                                           uses 1 12 pages of calculations. See Section 8.7 of Pollard (2002) for another presentation of
                                           Walther’s proof. By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids calculations.
                                                A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following. Using Crofton’s
                                           measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of µ(S) for all half-spaces S determines the
                                           µ-average distance fµ (x) to every point, x. We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian
                                           applied to fµ yields a constant times µ. Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation
                                           recovers µ.

## Complete Source Proof Text

The source proof of the proclaimed theorem is available and should be used by the prover. It is reproduced here from the TeX/PDF extraction, with minor whitespace normalization only.

```text
Let S be the set of closed half-spaces S ⊂ R^n.

The Cramer--Wold Theorem. Let μ and ν be Borel probability measures on R^n such that
μ(S) = ν(S) for all S ∈ S. Then μ = ν.

Proof. Let σ be the (infinite) Borel measure on S that is invariant under isometries,
normalized so that

  σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) = ‖x‖/2                                      (2.1)

for ‖x‖ = 1. The measure σ goes back to Crofton (1868) (in two dimensions); it can be
constructed as follows. Let Ω_{n-1} denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
S^{n-1} ⊂ R^n, and let λ denote Lebesgue measure on R. Write
ϕ : S^{n-1} × R → S for the map

  ϕ(ω,p) := {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}.

Then σ := α_n · ϕ_*(Ω_{n-1} × λ) for some constant α_n whose value does not concern us.
It is clear that σ is invariant under rotations about the origin and under reflections in
hyperplanes that pass through the origin. Translation invariance amounts to the property
that for y ∈ R^n, the pushforward by ϕ_y(ω,p) := ϕ(ω,p) - y is the same measure. But since

  ϕ(ω,p) - y
    = {x - y ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}
    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x + y> ≥ p}
    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p - <ω,y>}
    = ϕ(ω, p - <ω,y>),

isometry invariance of λ gives this property. The isometry invariance of σ implies that
σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) is a function of ‖x‖ alone; additivity for collinear segments shows that
it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose α_n so that (2.1) holds.

From (2.1) and isometry invariance, we have

  ‖x‖ = ∫_S |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dσ(S).

Integrating with respect to a signed measure μ on R^n with compact support, we obtain

  ∫_{R^n} ‖x‖ dμ(x)
    = ∫_S ∫_{R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dμ(x) dσ(S)
    = ∫_S [1_S(0)(1 - 2 μ(S)) + μ(S)] dσ(S).

The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another choice and subtracting, we get

  ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x)
    = ∫_S [(1_S(y) - 1_S(0))(1 - 2 μ(S))] dσ(S).

By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed measure μ.

Define

  f_μ(y) := ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x).

We have shown that the function S ↦ μ(S) determines f_μ. It remains to show that f_μ
determines μ.

The idea is that if n = 2m - 1 is odd, then Δ^m f_μ = c_m μ for some constant c_m, using
the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, Δ. This then establishes the Cramer--Wold
theorem in odd dimensions. But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension,
the Cramer--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well. That is, we may identify a
measure μ on R^{2m} with a measure μ' on R^{2m} × {0} ⊂ R^{2m+1}. The function S ↦ μ(S)
on half-spaces S ⊂ R^{2m} determines the values μ'(S') for half-spaces S' ⊂ R^{2m+1}.
Since this determines μ', the theorem follows for μ.

Recall also that if F : R^n → R is such that F(x) = G(‖x‖) depends only on r := ‖x‖, then

To show that f_μ determines ∫ g dμ for all g ∈ C_c^∞(R^{2m-1}), we now prove that with

  ∫_{R^{2m-1}} f_μ(y) (Δ^m g)(y) dλ(y)
```

```text
\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}


In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.

The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
the origin).
This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
the theorem,
no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
That changed with the publication of
\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
Gaussians.
Walther's proof depends on
a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
of Walther's proof.
By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
calculations.

A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
to every point, $x$.
We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
yields a constant times $\mu$.
Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.

\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}


Let $\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \subset\R^n$.

\proclaim The Cram\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
probability measures on $\R^n$ such that $\mu(S) = \nu(S)$ for all $S \in
\hfsp$. Then $\mu = \nu$.

\proof
Let
$\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\hfsp$ 
that is invariant under isometries, normalized so that
$$
\sigma\big(\{0 \in S, x \notin S\}\big) = \|x\|/2
\label e.distance
$$
for $\|x\|= 1$.
The measure $\sigma$ goes back to \ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it
can be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \ref b.SW:book/ for
a generalization.)
Let $\sfc_{n-1}$ denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
$\sphere^{n-1} \subset \R^n$, and let
$\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\R$.
Write $\varphi \colon \sphere^{n-1} \times \R \to \hfsp$ for the map
$$
\varphi(\omega, p)
:=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
\,.
$$
Then $\sigma := \alpha_n \cdot \varphi_*(\sfc_{n-1} \times \lambda)$ for some
constant $\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.
It is clear that $\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin
and under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.
Translation invariance
amounts to the property that for $y \in \R^n$, the pushforward by
$\varphi_y(\omega, p) := \varphi(\omega, p) - y$ is the same measure. But
since 
$$\eqaln{
\varphi(\omega, p) - y 
&= 
\bigl\{ x - y \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, {x + y} \ge p \bigr\}
\cr&=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p - \ip \omega, y \bigr\}
=
\varphi\bigl(\omega, p - \ip \omega, y\bigr)
\,,
}$$
isometry invariance of $\lambda$ gives this property.
The isometry invariance of $\sigma$ implies that $\sigma\big(\{0 \in S,\, x
\notin S\}\big)$ is a function of $\|x\|$ alone; additivity for collinear
segments shows that it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose $\alpha_n$
so that \ref e.distance/ holds.

From \ref e.distance/ and isometry invariance, we have
$$
\|x\| =
\int_\hfsp |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
Integrating with respect to a
signed measure $\mu$ on $\R^n$ with compact support, we obtain
$$
\int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \int_{\R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\mu(x) \,d\sigma(S)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[1_S(0)\big(1 - 2\mu(S)\big) + \mu(S)\Bigr] \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another
choice and subtracting, we get
$$
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\bigr)\bigl(1 - 2\mu(S)\bigr)\Bigr]
\,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed
measure, $\mu$.

Define
$$
f_\mu(y)
:=
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
\,.
$$
We have shown that the function $S \mapsto \mu(S)$ determines $f_\mu$. It
remains to show that $f_\mu$ determines $\mu$.

The idea is that if $n = 2m-1$ is odd, then $\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m
\mu$ for some constant $c_m$, using the fundamental solution of the
Laplacian, $\Delta$. This then establishes the Cram\'er--Wold theorem
in odd dimensions.
But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension, 
the Cram\'er--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well.
That is, we may identify a measure $\mu$ on $\R^{2m}$ with a measure $\mu'$
on $\R^{2m} \times \{0\} \subset \R^{2m+1}$. 
%Note that values on closed
%half-spaces determine values on open half-spaces by continuity.
%Thus, 
The function $S \mapsto
\mu(S)$ on half-spaces $S \subset \R^{2m}$ determines the values
$\mu'(S')$ for half-spaces $S' \subset \R^{2m+1}$. Since this determines
$\mu'$, the theorem follows for $\mu$.

We now show that

Recall Green's second identity, which says that for a
bounded domain $D \subset \R^n$ with $C^1$ boundary $\partial D$ having
outward unit normal $\n$ and two functions $\phi, \psi \in C^2(\overlinesl

$$

=
\int_{\partial D} (\phi \nabla_\n \psi - \psi \nabla_\n \phi)
\,.
$$

$$
(\Delta F)(x)
=
G''(r) + {n-1 \over r} G'(r)
\,.
$$
In particular, $\Delta r^k = k (k + n - 2) r^{k-2}$.
If the support of $\psi$ lies in the interior of a ball $B(\bfz, R)$ 
and $\phi(x) = r^k$ with $k > -n + 2$, then letting $D$ be $B(\bfz,
R) \setminus B(\bfz, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon \to 0$ shows that
$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \int_{\R^n} \psi \Delta \phi$. Similarly,
if $k = - n +2$, then 
$\int_{\R^n} \phi \Delta \psi = \beta_{n-1} \psi(\bfz)$, where
$\beta_{n-1}$ is the surface area of $\sphere^{n-1}$.

To show that $f_\mu$
determines $\int g \,d\mu$ for all $g \in C^\infty_{\csp}(\R^{2m-1})$, we
now prove that with $c_m := 2(-2\pi)^{m-1} (2m-2)!!$, where $!!$ denotes
the double factorial, we have
$$
\int g \,d\mu = c_m^{-1}
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y)
\,,
$$
where now
$\lambda$ denotes Lebesgue measure on $\R^{2m-1}$. Fubini's theorem
yields
$$
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} f_\mu(y) (\Delta^m g)(y) \,d\lambda(y) 
=
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
\, d\lambda(y) \,d\mu(x)
\,.
$$
Applying the preceding Green formulas (translated to $x$)
repeatedly to the inner integral, we obtain
$$\eqaln{
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) (\Delta^m g)(y)
\, d\lambda(y) 
&=
\int_{\R^{2m-1}} \Delta_y^{m-1}
\big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \Delta g(y) \,
d\lambda(y) 
\cr&=
c_m g(x) 
\,,
}$$
as desired.
\Qed

Our inversion formula $\mu = c_m^{-1} \Delta^m f_\mu$ in $\R^{2m-1}$
is similar to a well-known inversion formula for the Radon
transform due to \ref b.Radon/ and \ref b.John:book/, p.~13:
If $f \in C^1_{\csp}(\R^n)$, then writing $J(\omega, p) := \int_{\langle
\omega, x \rangle = p} f(x) \,dx$ for the integral of $f$ on a hyperplane
perpendicular to $\omega\in \sphere^{n-1}$, we have
$$
f(x) = \cases{\vadjust{\kern1pt}%
{1 \over 2} (2\pi)^{1-n} (-\Delta_x)^{(n-1)/2}
\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} J(\omega,\langle\omega, x\rangle)\,
d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
odd\cr
- (2\pi)^{-n} (-\Delta_x)^{(n-2)/2}
\int_{\sphere^{n-1}} \int_\R {dJ(\omega, p) \over p - \langle\omega,
x\rangle}\, d\Omega_{n-1}(\omega) &if $n$ is
even.\cr}
$$
%(Here, we are integrating with respect to unnormalized area measure.)

%for $n$ odd.
Apparently it was not realized until pointed out by \ref b.Renyi/ that the
theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ generalized the injectivity
results of Radon, John, and others.

The injectivity of the map $\mu \mapsto \int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)$ for
probability measures $\mu$ with finite first moment holds in other spaces
as well. On metric spaces of negative type, it is equivalent to strong
negative type. See Remark 3.4 of \ref b.L:dcov/ for details and references.
That paper also shows its relevance to statistics.
```

\title{A Calculus Proof of the Cram\'er--Wold Theorem}

\author{Russell Lyons and Kevin Zumbrun}

\abstract{We present a short, elementary proof not involving Fourier transforms
of the theorem of Cram\'er and Wold that a Borel probability measure is
determined by its values on half-spaces.
}

\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}


In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.

The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
the origin).
This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
the theorem,
no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
That changed with the publication of
\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
Gaussians.
Walther's proof depends on
a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
of Walther's proof.
By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
calculations.

A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
to every point, $x$.
We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
yields a constant times $\mu$.
Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.

\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}


Let $\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \subset\R^n$.

\proclaim The Cram\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
probability measures on $\R^n$ such that $\mu(S) = \nu(S)$ for all $S \in
\hfsp$. Then $\mu = \nu$.

\proof
Let
$\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\hfsp$ 
that is invariant under isometries, normalized so that
$$
\sigma\big(\{0 \in S, x \notin S\}\big) = \|x\|/2
\label e.distance
$$
for $\|x\|= 1$.
The measure $\sigma$ goes back to \ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it
can be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \ref b.SW:book/ for
a generalization.)
Let $\sfc_{n-1}$ denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
$\sphere^{n-1} \subset \R^n$, and let
$\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\R$.
Write $\varphi \colon \sphere^{n-1} \times \R \to \hfsp$ for the map
$$
\varphi(\omega, p)
:=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
\,.
$$
Then $\sigma := \alpha_n \cdot \varphi_*(\sfc_{n-1} \times \lambda)$ for some
constant $\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.
It is clear that $\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin
and under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.
Translation invariance
amounts to the property that for $y \in \R^n$, the pushforward by
$\varphi_y(\omega, p) := \varphi(\omega, p) - y$ is the same measure. But
since 
$$\eqaln{
\varphi(\omega, p) - y 
&= 
\bigl\{ x - y \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, {x + y} \ge p \bigr\}
\cr&=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p - \ip \omega, y \bigr\}
=
\varphi\bigl(\omega, p - \ip \omega, y\bigr)
\,,
}$$
isometry invariance of $\lambda$ gives this property.
The isometry invariance of $\sigma$ implies that $\sigma\big(\{0 \in S,\, x
\notin S\}\big)$ is a function of $\|x\|$ alone; additivity for collinear
segments shows that it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose $\alpha_n$
so that \ref e.distance/ holds.

From \ref e.distance/ and isometry invariance, we have
$$
\|x\| =
\int_\hfsp |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
Integrating with respect to a
signed measure $\mu$ on $\R^n$ with compact support, we obtain
$$
\int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \int_{\R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 \,d\mu(x) \,d\sigma(S)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[1_S(0)\big(1 - 2\mu(S)\big) + \mu(S)\Bigr] \,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another
choice and subtracting, we get
$$
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
=
\int_\hfsp \Bigl[\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\bigr)\bigl(1 - 2\mu(S)\bigr)\Bigr]
\,d\sigma(S)
\,.
$$
By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed
measure, $\mu$.

Define
$$
f_\mu(y)
:=
\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)
\,.
$$
We have shown that the function $S \mapsto \mu(S)$ determines $f_\mu$. It
remains to show that $f_\mu$ determines $\mu$.

The idea is that if $n = 2m-1$ is odd, then $\Delta^m f_\mu = c_m
\mu$ for some constant $c_m$, using the fundamental solution of the
Laplacian, $\Delta$. This then establishes the Cram\'er--Wold theorem
in odd dimensions.
But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension, 
the Cram\'er--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well.
That is, we may identify a measure $\mu$ on $\R^{2m}$ with a measure $\mu'$
on $\R^{2m} \times \{0\} \subset \R^{2m+1}$. 
%Note that values on closed
%half-spaces determine values on open half-spaces by continuity.
%Thus, 
The function $S \mapsto
\mu(S)$ on half-spaces $S \subset \R^{2m}$ determines the values
$\mu'(S')$ for half-spaces $S' \subset \R^{2m+1}$. Since this determines
$\mu'$, the theorem follows for $\mu$.

$$
%(Here, we are integrating with respect to unnormalized area measure.)
%This is from Helgason's remarks; in his book, he has a factor of 1/2 for

Apparently it was not realized until pointed out by \ref b.Renyi/ that the

The injectivity of the map $\mu \mapsto \int_{\R^n} \|x\| \,d\mu(x)$ for

\title{A Calculus Proof of the Cram\'er--Wold Theorem}

\author{Russell Lyons and Kevin Zumbrun}

\abstract{We present a short, elementary proof not involving Fourier transforms
of the theorem of Cram\'er and Wold that a Borel probability measure is
determined by its values on half-spaces.
}


\bottomII{Primary

\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}


In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.

The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
the origin).
This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
the theorem,
no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
That changed with the publication of
\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
Gaussians.
Walther's proof depends on
a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
of Walther's proof.
By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
calculations.

A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
to every point, $x$.
We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
yields a constant times $\mu$.
Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.

probability measures $\mu$ with finite first moment holds in other spaces
as well. On metric spaces of negative type, it is equivalent to strong
negative type. See Remark 3.4 of \ref b.L:dcov/ for details and references.
That paper also shows its relevance to statistics.

   193|\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}
   194|
   195|
   196|In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
   197|transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.
   198|
   199|The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
   200|measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
   201|assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
   202|the origin).
   203|This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
   204|generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
   205|textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
   206|the theorem,
   207|no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
   208|That changed with the publication of
   209|\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
   210|Gaussians.
   211|Walther's proof depends on
   212|a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
   213|calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
   214|of Walther's proof.
   215|By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
   216|calculations.
   217|
   218|A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
   219|Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
   220|for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
   221|to every point, $x$.
   222|We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
   223|yields a constant times $\mu$.
   224|Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.
   225|
   226|\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}
   227|
   228|
   229|Let $\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \subset\R^n$.
   230|
   231|\proclaim The Cram\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
   232|probability measures on $\R^n$ such that $\mu(S) = \nu(S)$ for all $S \in
   233|\hfsp$. Then $\mu = \nu$.
   234|
   235|\proof
   236|Let
   237|$\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\hfsp$ 
   238|that is invariant under isometries, normalized so that
   239|$$
   240|\sigma\big(\{0 \in S, x \notin S\}\big) = \|x\|/2
   241|\label e.distance
   242|$$
   243|for $\|x\|= 1$.
   244|The measure $\sigma$ goes back to \ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it
   245|can be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \ref b.SW:book/ for
   246|a generalization.)

   248|$\sphere^{n-1} \subset \R^n$, and let
   249|$\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\R$.
   250|Write $\varphi \colon \sphere^{n-1} \times \R \to \hfsp$ for the map
   251|$$
   252|\varphi(\omega, p)
   253|:=
   254|\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
   255|\,.
   256|$$
   257|Then $\sigma := \alpha_n \cdot \varphi_*(\sfc_{n-1} \times \lambda)$ for some
   258|constant $\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.
   259|It is clear that $\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin
   260|and under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.
   261|Translation invariance
   262|amounts to the property that for $y \in \R^n$, the pushforward by
   263|$\varphi_y(\omega, p) := \varphi(\omega, p) - y$ is the same measure. But
   264|since 
   265|$$\eqaln{
   266|\varphi(\omega, p) - y 
   267|&= 
   268|\bigl\{ x - y \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
   269|=
   270|\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, {x + y} \ge p \bigr\}
   271|\cr&=
   272|\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p - \ip \omega, y \bigr\}
   273|=
   274|\varphi\bigl(\omega, p - \ip \omega, y\bigr)
   275|\,,
   276|}$$

   279|\notin S\}\big)$ is a function of $\|x\|$ alone; additivity for collinear
   280|segments shows that it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose $\alpha_n$
   281|so that \ref e.distance/ holds.

   287|\,.

   296|\int_\hfsp \Bigl[1_S(0)\big(1 - 2\mu(S)\big) + \mu(S)\Bigr] \,d\sigma(S)
   297|\,.

   300|choice and subtracting, we get

   302|\int_{\R^n} \big(\|y - x\| - \|x\|\big) \,d\mu(x)

   304|\int_\hfsp \Bigl[\bigl(1_S(y) - 1_S(0)\bigr)\bigl(1 - 2\mu(S)\bigr)\Bigr]
   305|\,d\sigma(S)
   306|\,.

   309|measure, $\mu$.

   194|The source proof of the proclaimed theorem is available and should be used by the prover. It is reproduced here from the TeX/PDF extraction, with minor whitespace normalization only.

   196|```text
   197|Let S be the set of closed half-spaces S ⊂ R^n.
   198|
   199|The Cramer--Wold Theorem. Let μ and ν be Borel probability measures on R^n such that
   200|μ(S) = ν(S) for all S ∈ S. Then μ = ν.
   201|
   202|Proof. Let σ be the (infinite) Borel measure on S that is invariant under isometries,
   203|normalized so that
   204|
   205|  σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) = ‖x‖/2                                      (2.1)
   206|
   207|for ‖x‖ = 1. The measure σ goes back to Crofton (1868) (in two dimensions); it can be
   208|constructed as follows. Let Ω_{n-1} denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
   209|S^{n-1} ⊂ R^n, and let λ denote Lebesgue measure on R. Write
   210|ϕ : S^{n-1} × R → S for the map
   211|
   212|  ϕ(ω,p) := {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}.
   213|
   214|Then σ := α_n · ϕ_*(Ω_{n-1} × λ) for some constant α_n whose value does not concern us.
   215|It is clear that σ is invariant under rotations about the origin and under reflections in
   216|hyperplanes that pass through the origin. Translation invariance amounts to the property

                                                    A Calculus Proof of the Cramér–Wold Theorem

                                                                       by Russell Lyons and Kevin Zumbrun




arXiv:1607.03206v2 [math.PR] 24 Apr 2017
                                                     Abstract. We present a short, elementary proof not involving Fourier transforms
                                                     of the theorem of Cramér and Wold that a Borel probability measure is determined
                                                     by its values on half-spaces.




                                                                                     §1. Introduction.
                                                In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier transforms, of a
                                           theorem of Cramér and Wold.
                                                The fundamental theorem of Cramér and Wold (1936) states that a Borel probability
                                           measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently,
                                           by its projections to lines through the origin). This theorem is proved easily with the aid of
                                           Fourier analysis. However, generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
                                           textbook of Billingsley (1995) that despite the elementary statement of the theorem, no proof
                                           was known that did not use Fourier transforms. That changed with the publication of Walther
                                           (1997), who used Gaussians. Walther’s proof depends on a nice idea, but its implementation
                                           uses 1 12 pages of calculations. See Section 8.7 of Pollard (2002) for another presentation of
                                           Walther’s proof. By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids calculations.
                                                A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following. Using Crofton’s
                                           measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of µ(S) for all half-spaces S determines the
                                           µ-average distance fµ (x) to every point, x. We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian
                                           applied to fµ yields a constant times µ. Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation
                                           recovers µ.

                                           Key words and phrases. Distributions of probability measures, Radon transform, integral geometry.
                                           Research partially supported by NSF grants DMS-1007244 and DMS-1400555.

    25|                                           measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently,

Let S be the set of closed half-spaces S ⊂ R^n.

The Cramer--Wold Theorem. Let μ and ν be Borel probability measures on R^n such that
μ(S) = ν(S) for all S ∈ S. Then μ = ν.

Proof. Let σ be the (infinite) Borel measure on S that is invariant under isometries,
normalized so that

  σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) = ‖x‖/2                                      (2.1)

for ‖x‖ = 1. The measure σ goes back to Crofton (1868) (in two dimensions); it can be
constructed as follows. Let Ω_{n-1} denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
S^{n-1} ⊂ R^n, and let λ denote Lebesgue measure on R. Write
ϕ : S^{n-1} × R → S for the map

  ϕ(ω,p) := {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}.

Then σ := α_n · ϕ_*(Ω_{n-1} × λ) for some constant α_n whose value does not concern us.
It is clear that σ is invariant under rotations about the origin and under reflections in
hyperplanes that pass through the origin. Translation invariance amounts to the property
that for y ∈ R^n, the pushforward by ϕ_y(ω,p) := ϕ(ω,p) - y is the same measure. But since

  ϕ(ω,p) - y
    = {x - y ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}
    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x + y> ≥ p}
    = {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p - <ω,y>}
    = ϕ(ω, p - <ω,y>),

isometry invariance of λ gives this property. The isometry invariance of σ implies that
σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) is a function of ‖x‖ alone; additivity for collinear segments shows that
it is a linear function. Thus, we may choose α_n so that (2.1) holds.

From (2.1) and isometry invariance, we have

  ‖x‖ = ∫_S |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dσ(S).

Integrating with respect to a signed measure μ on R^n with compact support, we obtain

  ∫_{R^n} ‖x‖ dμ(x)
    = ∫_S ∫_{R^n} |1_S(0) - 1_S(x)|^2 dμ(x) dσ(S)
    = ∫_S [1_S(0)(1 - 2 μ(S)) + μ(S)] dσ(S).

The choice of 0 was arbitrary, so making another choice and subtracting, we get

  ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x)
    = ∫_S [(1_S(y) - 1_S(0))(1 - 2 μ(S))] dσ(S).

By taking a limit, we see that this equation holds for every finite signed measure μ.

Define

  f_μ(y) := ∫_{R^n} (‖y - x‖ - ‖x‖) dμ(x).

We have shown that the function S ↦ μ(S) determines f_μ. It remains to show that f_μ
determines μ.

The idea is that if n = 2m - 1 is odd, then Δ^m f_μ = c_m μ for some constant c_m, using
the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, Δ. This then establishes the Cramer--Wold
theorem in odd dimensions. But since an even dimension embeds in the next higher dimension,
the Cramer--Wold theorem follows in even dimensions as well. That is, we may identify a
measure μ on R^{2m} with a measure μ' on R^{2m} × {0} ⊂ R^{2m+1}. The function S ↦ μ(S)
on half-spaces S ⊂ R^{2m} determines the values μ'(S') for half-spaces S' ⊂ R^{2m+1}.
Since this determines μ', the theorem follows for μ.

```text
\bsection{Introduction}{s.intro}


In this note, we give a brief and elementary proof, not involving Fourier
transforms, of a theorem of Cram\'er and Wold.

The fundamental theorem of \ref b.CramerWold/ states that a Borel probability
measure on Euclidean space is determined by the values it
assigns to all half-spaces (equivalently, by its projections to lines through
the origin).
This theorem is proved easily with the aid of Fourier analysis. However,
generations of probabilists have learned from the editions of the
textbook of \ref b.Billingsley:PM/ that despite the elementary statement of
the theorem,
no proof was known that did not use Fourier transforms.
That changed with the publication of
\ref b.walther:withAdd/, who used
Gaussians.
Walther's proof depends on
a nice idea, but its implementation uses $1 {1 \over 2}$ pages of
calculations. See Section 8.7 of \ref b.Pollard/ for another presentation
of Walther's proof.
By contrast, our proof uses only natural constructions and avoids
calculations.

A brief and somewhat inaccurate outline of our proof is the following.
Using Crofton's measure on half-spaces, we show that knowledge of $\mu(S)$
for all half-spaces $S$ determines the $\mu$-average distance $f_\mu(x)$
to every point, $x$.
We then show that a suitable power of the Laplacian applied to $f_\mu$
yields a constant times $\mu$.
Thus, integral geometry combined with differentiation recovers $\mu$.

\bsection{Proof}{s.proof}


Let $\hfsp$ be the set of closed half-spaces $S \subset\R^n$.

\proclaim The Cram\'er--Wold Theorem. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be Borel
probability measures on $\R^n$ such that $\mu(S) = \nu(S)$ for all $S \in
\hfsp$. Then $\mu = \nu$.

\proof
Let
$\sigma$ be the (infinite) Borel measure on $\hfsp$ 
that is invariant under isometries, normalized so that
$$
\sigma\big(\{0 \in S, x \notin S\}\big) = \|x\|/2
\label e.distance
$$
for $\|x\|= 1$.
The measure $\sigma$ goes back to \ref b.Crofton/ (in two dimensions); it
can be constructed as follows. (See Theorem 5.1.1 of \ref b.SW:book/ for
a generalization.)
Let $\sfc_{n-1}$ denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
$\sphere^{n-1} \subset \R^n$, and let
$\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\R$.
Write $\varphi \colon \sphere^{n-1} \times \R \to \hfsp$ for the map
$$
\varphi(\omega, p)
:=
\bigl\{ x \in \R^n \st \ip \omega, x \ge p \bigr\}
\,.
$$
Then $\sigma := \alpha_n \cdot \varphi_*(\sfc_{n-1} \times \lambda)$ for some
constant $\alpha_n$ whose value does not concern us.
It is clear that $\sigma$ is invariant under rotations about the origin
and under reflections in hyperplanes that pass through the origin.

from __future__ import annotations

import json

PDF_READ_DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS = 24_000
PDF_READ_MAX_CHARS = 120_000


def check_document_requirements() -> bool:
    return True


def formalization_document_inspect_tool(
    path: str,
    *,
    cwd: str = "",
    project_root: str = "",
    include_text: bool = False,
) -> str:
    root = (
        project_root
        or os.getenv("EPFLEMMA_PROJECT_ROOT", "")
        or os.getenv("OPENGAUSS_PROJECT_ROOT", "")
        or cwd
        or os.getcwd()
    )
    payload = inspect_formalization_document(
        path,
        project_root=root,
        cwd=cwd or root,
    )
    if not include_text:
        payload.pop("extracted_text", None)
    return json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False)


def read_pdf_tool(
    path: str,
    *,
    cwd: str = "",
    project_root: str = "",
    max_chars: int = PDF_READ_DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS,
) -> str:
    root = (
        project_root
        or os.getenv("EPFLEMMA_PROJECT_ROOT", "")
        or os.getenv("OPENGAUSS_PROJECT_ROOT", "")
        or cwd
        or os.getcwd()
    )
    payload = inspect_formalization_document(
        path,
        project_root=root,
        cwd=cwd or root,
    )
    if payload.get("source_kind") != "pdf":
        return json.dumps(
            {
                "success": False,
                "error": "read_pdf only accepts project-local .pdf files",
                "source_kind": payload.get("source_kind"),
                "source_relative": payload.get("source_relative"),
            },
            ensure_ascii=False,
        )
    try:
        limit = int(max_chars or PDF_READ_DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS)
    except Exception:
        limit = PDF_READ_DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS
    limit = max(1_000, min(limit, PDF_READ_MAX_CHARS))
    extracted = str(payload.get("extracted_text", "") or "")
    payload["extracted_text"] = extracted[:limit]
    payload["text_truncated"] = len(extracted) > limit
    payload["text_limit_chars"] = limit
    return json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False)
```

   196	```text
   197	Let S be the set of closed half-spaces S ⊂ R^n.
   198	
   199	The Cramer--Wold Theorem. Let μ and ν be Borel probability measures on R^n such that
   200	μ(S) = ν(S) for all S ∈ S. Then μ = ν.
   201	
   202	Proof. Let σ be the (infinite) Borel measure on S that is invariant under isometries,
   203	normalized so that
   204	
   205	  σ({0 ∈ S, x ∉ S}) = ‖x‖/2                                      (2.1)
   206	
   207	for ‖x‖ = 1. The measure σ goes back to Crofton (1868) (in two dimensions); it can be
   208	constructed as follows. Let Ω_{n-1} denote hypersurface area measure on the unit sphere
   209	S^{n-1} ⊂ R^n, and let λ denote Lebesgue measure on R. Write
   210	ϕ : S^{n-1} × R → S for the map
   211	
   212	  ϕ(ω,p) := {x ∈ R^n | <ω,x> ≥ p}.
   213	
   214	Then σ := α_n · ϕ_*(Ω_{n-1} × λ) for some constant α_n whose value does not concern us.
